opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was a real turning point for us. For many years my team was very deep in GANs. We did work like pix2pixHD, vid2vid, GauGAN, and we were proud of it. GANs gave you really sharp images and fast sampling, and for a while they were the best tool we had for high-quality image synthesis.

But I started asking myself a simple question: if I give this method ten times more data and ten times more compute, does it reliably get ten times better? With GANs the honest answer was often no. Training is a min-max game between two networks, and it's fragile. When you scale up the model or the dataset, you spend a lot of your energy just keeping training stable: tuning hyperparameters, adding regularizers, babysitting runs, dealing with mode collapse. Every new scale felt like a new research project just to make it converge. That's not a good property if you believe, as I do, that progress in AI comes largely from scaling.

Around the same time, we saw diffusion models and autoregressive models showing a very different behavior. The training objective is basically a regression or likelihood-style loss. It's boring in a good way. You add more data and more compute and the loss goes down predictably, and the samples get better. They cover the data distribution much better instead of collapsing onto a few modes. Sampling was slower at first, but that's an engineering problem you can attack later with distillation and better solvers. Instability at scale is much harder to engineer away.

So it was a strategic decision, not because GANs were bad ideas. Adversarial training is still a beautiful idea, and it shows up again in things like distillation. But as the main engine, I wanted something that would let us ride the scaling curve. Moving the team was not easy, because people had built expertise and reputations around GANs. I tried to explain that our goal isn't a particular technique; our goal is building generative models that can understand and simulate the world. If a different tool scales better toward that goal, we should switch, and switch early rather than late.

Looking back, that shift is what made our later work on large video and world foundation models possible. If we had stayed with GANs, I don't think we could have trained models at that scale.

r001.rationale: Liu says progress comes largely from scaling and favors simpler regression or likelihood-style objectives that improve predictably with more data and compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Jia-Bin Huang or describe using multiple discriminators with different weights and a shared generator.

r003.rationale: Liu describes repeated difficulties keeping GAN training stable as scale increased and says that this motivated moving the team away from GANs.

fable-5.1.text:
Around 2020, 2021, my team at NVIDIA was still quite deep in GANs. We had done pix2pixHD, vid2vid, SPADE, GauGAN, and those models worked, people loved them. But I kept running the same thought experiment: if I had ten times the data and ten times the compute, would this model get ten times better? And for GANs the honest answer was no. Training was unstable, and the instability got worse as you scaled the generator and the discriminator together. You would spend weeks of engineering just to keep the two networks from collapsing, and in the end you got a model that worked beautifully on faces or on one dataset, but would not simply absorb more data and become more general.

Meanwhile I was watching what was happening in language. GPT-2, then GPT-3. The lesson there was very simple. You pick an objective that is stable, like maximum likelihood, you make the model bigger, you feed it more data, and the curve just keeps going. No adversarial game, no mode collapse, just a loss that goes down predictably. That predictability is what scalability really means. It is not just that you can make the model bigger, it is that you can forecast what you will get before you spend the money.

So I asked, what is the equivalent of that for images and video? Diffusion models gave us that answer. The objective is essentially a regression, a denoising loss, which is very close in spirit to likelihood training. It is boring in a good way. You can throw more data and more GPUs at it and it improves in a way you can plan around. Once I saw that, I felt it was my responsibility to move the team, even though GANs were our reputation. Many people on the team had built their careers on them, so it was not easy emotionally. But research is about betting on the trajectory, not on the past. We shifted the group, started working on what became eDiff-I and later the video and world model work, and I have not regretted it. GANs taught us a lot, especially about perceptual quality and fast sampling, and some of those ideas come back as distillation. But as the backbone of a scaling program, they could not carry the weight.

r001.rationale: Liu says GANs did not improve predictably with more data and compute, while simpler, stable objectives scale reliably; he describes betting on that trajectory.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Jia-Bin Huang or a proposal involving multiple discriminators competing against a shared generator.

r003.rationale: Liu describes recurring instability and failed scaling expectations for GANs, then says this led him to move the team to diffusion research.

astra-6.text:
For me, scalability became a question of whether we could keep improving a model by giving it more data and more compute. With GANs, you’re training two networks—the generator and the discriminator—and you need to keep that interaction stable. Putting more resources into training doesn’t necessarily translate into a better model; you can end up spending a lot of effort balancing the two networks.

That made me rethink what we should focus on as a team. Rather than just asking how to improve the next GAN, I wanted us to look for approaches where the training was more predictable and additional resources could more reliably lead to better results. It wasn’t that GANs stopped being interesting. Scalability became a more important criterion for choosing our research direction.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, scalability became a question of whether we could keep improving a model by adding more data and compute. With GANs, you have a generator and a discriminator that have to learn together, and that balance can be difficult to maintain. You can make the networks bigger, but that doesn’t necessarily translate into predictable improvements.

So I started to think less about how to make a particular GAN better and more about which approach would let us scale reliably. Diffusion models offered a more stable training objective and a clearer path to benefiting from additional compute. That was the motivation for moving the team: we wanted to work on an approach where scaling could become a dependable way to improve quality.
